name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q01 - Sequence of steps in balancing redox reactions

questiontext.text:
In balancing a chemical equation for a redox process in an acidic aqueous solution using the oxidation number method, consider the following procedural steps:

(I) Balance the total ionic charges on both sides of the equation by adding \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ions.
(II) Write the correct skeletal chemical formulas for all reactants and products.
(III) Balance hydrogen atoms by adding appropriate numbers of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) molecules, then verify oxygen atom balance.
(IV) Assign oxidation numbers to all elements and identify the atoms undergoing change in oxidation state.
(V) Calculate the increase and decrease in oxidation number per atom and multiply by suitable integers to equalize the total increase and decrease.

Which of the following represents the correct sequential order of steps from beginning to end?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Initial Skeletal Formulation
The oxidation number method begins by writing down the correct skeletal chemical formula for each reactant and product involved in the reaction.

Step 2: Assigning Oxidation Numbers and Identifying Changes
The next step requires assigning oxidation numbers to every element in the equation according to standard rules, identifying which species undergo oxidation (increase in oxidation number) and which undergo reduction (decrease in oxidation number).

Step 3: Equalizing Increase and Decrease in Oxidation Number
The increase in oxidation number per atom for the reductant and the decrease in oxidation number per atom for the oxidant are calculated. Appropriate integer stoichiometric coefficients are placed before the formulas so that the total increase in oxidation number exactly equals the total decrease.

Step 4: Balancing Charge in Acidic Medium
Because the reaction takes place in an acidic aqueous medium, \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ions are added to the appropriate side of the equation so that the net ionic charges on the reactant side and product side become identical.

Step 5: Balancing Hydrogen and Oxygen Atoms
Finally, the number of hydrogen atoms is balanced by adding \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) molecules to the deficient side, and the equation is checked to ensure that the number of oxygen atoms is equal on both sides.

Step 6: Final Answer
The correct chronological sequence of operations is writing skeletal formulas, followed by assigning oxidation numbers, equalizing oxidation number changes, balancing ionic charges with hydrogen ions, and finally balancing hydrogen and oxygen with water molecules: (II) → (IV) → (V) → (I) → (III).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q02 - Conceptual evolution of the definition of oxidation

questiontext.text:
Consider the conceptual milestones in the historical and pedagogical development of the definition of 'oxidation' in chemistry:

(I) Electronic transfer concept: Oxidation is defined as the loss of electron(s) by any chemical species.
(II) Limited classical definition: Oxidation is defined strictly as the addition of oxygen to an element or a compound.
(III) Modern unified concept: Oxidation is viewed as an increase in the oxidation number or a decrease in electron density around an atom.
(IV) Broadened classical definition: Oxidation is expanded to include the removal of hydrogen or the removal of electropositive elements.

Which of the following represents the correct chronological and conceptual progression of the term 'oxidation'?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Earliest Classical Definition
Originally, the term oxidation was coined strictly to describe the direct combination of atmospheric oxygen with elements or compounds, such as \(2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO}\).

Step 2: Extension to Hydrogen and Electropositive Elements
As knowledge expanded through reactions like the combustion of methane and the oxidation of hydrogen sulfide, chemists reinterpreted oxidation to include the removal of hydrogen as well as the removal of other electropositive elements (such as potassium from potassium ferrocyanide).

Step 3: Formulation of the Electron Transfer Model
Upon recognizing that ionic solids consist of discrete cations and anions formed through redox changes (such as \(2\mathrm{Na} + \mathrm{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaCl}\)), oxidation was fundamentally reformulated as the loss of one or more electrons by any interacting species.

Step 4: Generalized Oxidation Number and Electron Density Description
To track electron shifts in covalent molecules where formal electron transfer is incomplete, the concept of oxidation number was established. More recently, oxidation has been unified as an increase in oxidation state or a decrease in electron density around the atom.

Step 5: Final Answer
The sequential evolution proceeds from the limited classical definition of oxygen addition, to the broadened classical definition involving hydrogen removal, followed by the electronic transfer concept, and finally the generalized oxidation number and electron density concept: (II) → (IV) → (I) → (III).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q03 - Balancing reduction half-reaction in basic medium

questiontext.text:
When balancing the reduction half-reaction of permanganate ion to manganese dioxide in a basic aqueous solution using the half-reaction method:

\[\mathrm{MnO}_4^-(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_2(\mathrm{s})\]

consider the following sequence of operations:

(I) Add \(4\mathrm{H}^+\) ions to the left side to balance hydrogen atoms.
(II) Add \(2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) molecules to the right side to balance oxygen atoms.
(III) Add \(4\mathrm{OH}^-\) ions to both sides of the equation and combine \(\mathrm{H}^+\) and \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) on the left side to form \(4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).
(IV) Cancel duplicate water molecules to obtain \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_2 + 4\mathrm{OH}^-\).
(V) Add \(3\mathrm{e}^-\) to the left side to balance electrical charges.

Which of the following represents the correct logical sequence of steps?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Balancing Oxygen Atoms with Water
In the skeletal half-reaction \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^- \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_2\), manganese is already balanced. The reactant side has 4 oxygen atoms and the product side has 2. Two water molecules must first be added to the product side:
\(\mathrm{MnO}_4^- \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).

Step 2: Balancing Hydrogen Atoms with Hydrogen Ions
To balance the 4 hydrogen atoms introduced on the right side, \(4\mathrm{H}^+\) ions are added to the left side:
\(\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 4\mathrm{H}^+ \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).

Step 3: Conversion to Basic Medium
Because the reaction takes place in basic medium, for every \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ion present, an equal number of \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) ions (\(4\mathrm{OH}^-\)) must be added to both sides of the equation. On the left side, \(4\mathrm{H}^+ + 4\mathrm{OH}^-\) combine to form \(4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\):
\(\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + 4\mathrm{OH}^-\).

Step 4: Simplifying Water Molecules
Cancelling two water molecules from both sides gives the simplified atom-balanced equation:
\(\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_2 + 4\mathrm{OH}^-\).

Step 5: Balancing Electric Charge with Electrons
The net charge on the left is \(-1\) and on the right is \(-4\). To balance charges, \(3\mathrm{e}^-\) must be added to the left side, yielding the fully balanced reduction half-reaction:
\(\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + 3\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO}_2 + 4\mathrm{OH}^-\).

Step 6: Final Answer
The correct sequence of operations is balancing oxygen with water, balancing hydrogen with hydrogen ions, converting to basic medium by adding hydroxide ions, cancelling duplicate water molecules, and finally adding electrons to balance charge: (II) → (I) → (III) → (IV) → (V).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q04 - Chronological stages of competitive zinc copper reaction

questiontext.text:
In a laboratory experiment investigating competitive electron transfer, a clean strip of metallic zinc is placed into an aqueous solution of copper nitrate. Consider the following observations and operations:

(I) The intensity of the deep blue colour of the solution begins to diminish, and a reddish-brown crust starts depositing on the surface of the zinc rod.
(II) The clean zinc strip is placed into the deep blue copper nitrate solution.
(III) Addition of aqueous ammonia to make the solution alkaline followed by passing \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\) gas produces a characteristic white precipitate.
(IV) The blue colour completely disappears leaving a colourless solution with metallic copper deposited on the zinc rod.

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of experimental observations and procedures?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Placement of Zinc in Solution
The experiment commences when a polished, clean strip of metallic zinc is immersed in a beaker filled with an aqueous copper nitrate solution, which has a characteristic deep blue colour due to hydrated \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions.

Step 2: Progress of Electron Transfer and Color Fading
As electron transfer initiates, zinc atoms lose electrons to form \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions while copper ions gain electrons to form elemental copper. The intensity of the blue colour gradually fades as the concentration of \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) decreases, and a reddish-brown layer of copper metal begins coating the zinc rod.

Step 3: Complete Consumption of Copper Ions
After approximately one hour, the blue colour completely disappears, leaving a water-clear, colourless solution containing \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions and an appreciable deposit of reddish metallic copper on the rod.

Step 4: Confirmatory Chemical Test for Product Ions
To verify the formation of \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\) ions in the colourless solution, aqueous ammonia is added to make the medium alkaline, followed by bubbling hydrogen sulfide gas (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\)), which results in the immediate precipitation of white zinc sulfide (\(\mathrm{ZnS}\)).

Step 5: Final Answer
The correct chronological sequence is immersing the zinc strip, observing the fading of blue colour with copper deposition, complete disappearance of blue colour, and chemical confirmation with alkaline hydrogen sulfide: (II) → (I) → (IV) → (III).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q05 - Ordering of halogens by increasing oxidizing power

questiontext.text:
Based on the halogen activity series and their standard electrode reduction potentials at \(298\mathrm{\ K}\):

\[\mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{F}_2/\mathrm{F}^-) = +2.87\mathrm{\ V}, \quad \mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{Cl}_2/\mathrm{Cl}^-) = +1.36\mathrm{\ V}, \quad \mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{Br}_2/\mathrm{Br}^-) = +1.09\mathrm{\ V}, \quad \mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{I}_2/\mathrm{I}^-) = +0.54\mathrm{\ V}\]

Which of the following represents the correct sequence of halogens arranged in strictly increasing order of their power as oxidising agents?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Principle of Oxidising Strength and Electrode Potential
The power of an element to act as an oxidising agent corresponds to its tendency to gain electrons and undergo reduction. A higher, more positive standard reduction potential (\(\mathrm{E}^\circ\)) indicates a greater driving force for reduction and hence a stronger oxidising ability.

Step 2: Comparison of Standard Reduction Potentials
Listing the given standard electrode potentials for the reduction half-reactions \(\mathrm{X}_2 + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{X}^-\):
• For iodine (\(\mathrm{I}_2\)): \(\mathrm{E}^\circ = +0.54\mathrm{\ V}\)
• For bromine (\(\mathrm{Br}_2\)): \(\mathrm{E}^\circ = +1.09\mathrm{\ V}\)
• For chlorine (\(\mathrm{Cl}_2\)): \(\mathrm{E}^\circ = +1.36\mathrm{\ V}\)
• For fluorine (\(\mathrm{F}_2\)): \(\mathrm{E}^\circ = +2.87\mathrm{\ V}\)

Step 3: Verification with Halogen Displacement Behavior
Chlorine displaces both bromide and iodide from aqueous halides (\(\mathrm{Cl}_2 + 2\mathrm{Br}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cl}^- + \mathrm{Br}_2\)). Bromine displaces iodide (\(\mathrm{Br}_2 + 2\mathrm{I}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Br}^- + \mathrm{I}_2\)). Fluorine is so reactive that it oxidises the oxygen of water directly. Thus, oxidising power decreases down group 17 from fluorine to iodine.

Step 4: Final Answer
Arranging in strictly increasing order of oxidising power gives iodine as the weakest oxidant and fluorine as the strongest oxidant: \(\mathrm{I}_2 < \mathrm{Br}_2 < \mathrm{Cl}_2 < \mathrm{F}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q06 - Ordering of metals by increasing reducing power

questiontext.text:
Given the standard electrode reduction potentials at \(298\mathrm{\ K}\):

\[\mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{Ag}^+/\mathrm{Ag}) = +0.80\mathrm{\ V}, \quad \mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{Hg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Hg}) = +0.79\mathrm{\ V}, \quad \mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}/\mathrm{Cr}) = -0.74\mathrm{\ V},\]

\[\mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Mg}) = -2.37\mathrm{\ V}, \quad \mathrm{E}^\circ(\mathrm{K}^+/\mathrm{K}) = -2.93\mathrm{\ V}\]

Which of the following represents the correct sequence of these metals arranged in strictly increasing order of their reducing power?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Principle of Reducing Power and Reduction Potential
A reducing agent acts by donating electrons and is itself oxidised. A more negative standard reduction potential (\(\mathrm{E}^\circ\)) indicates that the redox couple has a higher tendency to lose electrons than the standard hydrogen electrode, making the elemental metal a stronger reducing agent. Conversely, a more positive reduction potential signifies a weaker reducing agent.

Step 2: Tabulating Potential Values
Sorting the given standard reduction potentials from most positive to most negative:
• \(\mathrm{Ag}^+/\mathrm{Ag} = +0.80\mathrm{\ V}\)
• \(\mathrm{Hg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Hg} = +0.79\mathrm{\ V}\)
• \(\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}/\mathrm{Cr} = -0.74\mathrm{\ V}\)
• \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Mg} = -2.37\mathrm{\ V}\)
• \(\mathrm{K}^+/\mathrm{K} = -2.93\mathrm{\ V}\)

Step 3: Establishing the Sequence of Reducing Power
Since reducing power increases as \(\mathrm{E}^\circ\) becomes more negative:
Silver has the most positive reduction potential (\(+0.80\mathrm{\ V}\)) and is the weakest reducing agent.
Mercury is next (\(+0.79\mathrm{\ V}\)).
Chromium is stronger (\(-0.74\mathrm{\ V}\)).
Magnesium is stronger still (\(-2.37\mathrm{\ V}\)).
Potassium has the most negative potential (\(-2.93\mathrm{\ V}\)) and is the strongest reducing agent.

Step 4: Final Answer
The metals arranged in increasing order of reducing power follow the sequence: \(\mathrm{Ag} < \mathrm{Hg} < \mathrm{Cr} < \mathrm{Mg} < \mathrm{K}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q07 - Arrangement of sulfur species by oxidation number

questiontext.text:
Consider the following sulfur-containing species:

(I) Hydrogen sulfide, \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\)
(II) Tetrathionate ion, \(\mathrm{S}_4\mathrm{O}_6^{2-}\)
(III) Elemental rhombic sulfur, \(\mathrm{S}_8\)
(IV) Sulfite ion, \(\mathrm{SO}_3^{2-}\)
(V) Sulfate ion, \(\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}\)

Which of the following represents the correct sequence of these species arranged in strictly increasing order of the oxidation state (or average oxidation state) of sulfur?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Calculation for Hydrogen Sulfide (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\))
Hydrogen bonded to a non-metal exhibits an oxidation state of \(+1\).
\(2(+1) + x = 0 \implies x = -2\).
Thus, sulfur in \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\) has an oxidation number of \(-2\).

Step 2: Calculation for Elemental Sulfur (\(\mathrm{S}_8\))
In elemental or uncombined homoatomic forms, each atom bears an oxidation number of zero. Thus, sulfur in \(\mathrm{S}_8\) has an oxidation number of \(0\).

Step 3: Calculation for Tetrathionate Ion (\(\mathrm{S}_4\mathrm{O}_6^{2-}\))
Oxygen is assigned an oxidation state of \(-2\). Equating the algebraic sum to the ion charge of \(-2\):
\(4x + 6(-2) = -2 \implies 4x - 12 = -2 \implies 4x = +10 \implies x = +2.5\).
Thus, sulfur in \(\mathrm{S}_4\mathrm{O}_6^{2-}\) has an average oxidation number of \(+2.5\).

Step 4: Calculation for Sulfite Ion (\(\mathrm{SO}_3^{2-}\))
Equating the sum to the net charge of \(-2\):
\(x + 3(-2) = -2 \implies x - 6 = -2 \implies x = +4\).
Thus, sulfur in \(\mathrm{SO}_3^{2-}\) has an oxidation number of \(+4\).

Step 5: Calculation for Sulfate Ion (\(\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}\))
Equating the sum to the net charge of \(-2\):
\(x + 4(-2) = -2 \implies x - 8 = -2 \implies x = +6\).
Thus, sulfur in \(\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}\) has an oxidation number of \(+6\).

Step 6: Final Answer
Arranging in strictly increasing numerical order: \(-2 < 0 < +2.5 < +4 < +6\). The corresponding sequence of species is (I) → (III) → (II) → (IV) → (V).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MCQ_Q08 - Procedural stages in an iodometric redox titration

questiontext.text:
In the quantitative iodometric titration of cupric ions (\(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\)) using standard sodium thiosulfate (\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) and starch indicator, consider the following experimental stages:

(I) Freshly prepared starch indicator is introduced into the pale straw-yellow solution, forming an intense deep-blue starch-iodine adsorption complex.
(II) Standard sodium thiosulfate solution is run from the burette into the liberated iodine solution until the dark reddish-brown colour fades to a pale straw-yellow.
(III) An excess of potassium iodide is added to the aqueous copper(II) solution, precipitating white cuprous iodide (\(\mathrm{Cu}_2\mathrm{I}_2\)) and liberating molecular iodine.
(IV) Titration with standard thiosulfate is continued dropwise until the deep-blue colour completely discharges, signalling the stoichiometric end point.

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of stages during this analytical procedure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Liberation of Iodine by Reaction with Iodide
The procedure begins by adding excess potassium iodide (\(\mathrm{KI}\)) to an aqueous solution of \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions. Cupric ions oxidise iodide according to the redox reaction:
\(2\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{I}^-(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}_2\mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{aq})\).
This reaction precipitates cuprous iodide as a white solid and releases an equimolar quantity of iodine, imparting an intense reddish-brown colour to the suspension.

Step 2: Pre-titration of Liberated Iodine
The liberated iodine is titrated against standard sodium thiosulfate (\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)). The reaction is:
\(\mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_3^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{I}^-(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{S}_4\mathrm{O}_6^{2-}(\mathrm{aq})\).
Thiosulfate is added until the dark reddish-brown colour of iodine is reduced to a faint pale straw-yellow.

Step 3: Timely Addition of Starch Indicator
Starch is not added at the beginning because high concentrations of iodine can irreversibly coagulate or bind to starch. When the solution reaches the pale straw-yellow stage, starch solution is introduced, immediately producing an intense, dark blue colour due to the formation of the starch-triiodide complex.

Step 4: Final Titration to End Point
Thiosulfate addition is resumed drop by drop with vigorous swirling until the final trace of iodine is converted to iodide ions, resulting in the sharp and permanent disappearance of the blue colour at the equivalence point.

Step 5: Final Answer
The correct chronological order of stages is generation of molecular iodine, pre-titration to straw-yellow colour, addition of starch indicator, and final discharge of blue colour: (III) → (II) → (I) → (IV).
